1.title: Authorization Mechanisms
1.text: Welcome to Module fifteen: Authorization Mechanisms. This module covers the task statement: apply authorization mechanisms. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Create custom I A M (Identity and Access Management) policies when a managed policy does not meet the needs. Store application and database credentials in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store. Give database users, groups and roles access in Amazon Redshift. Manage permissions through A W S Lake Formation for Redshift, E M R (Elastic MapReduce), Athena and S three. Choose role-based, tag-based and attribute-based authorization. Write policies that follow least privilege.

1.title: Case Check-In: Kestrel Freight Draws the Lines
1.text: Our running case is Kestrel Freight. Kestrel Freight Draws the Lines. Dispatchers may read live truck data, never invoices. Finance may read invoices but not customer phone numbers. E U analysts may see only E U customers' rows. Your job: grant exactly what each group needs and nothing more.

1.title: Custom IAM Policies
1.text: Custom I A M Policies. A W S managed policy. Created and updated by A W S for common jobs (for example Amazon S three read only access): quick, but often too broad. Customer managed policy. Your own reusable policy: versioned, attachable to many identities: the right choice when a managed policy does not fit. Inline policy. Embedded in one identity: for a strict one-to-one relationship. Resource-based policy. Attached to the resource (bucket, key, queue, secret) with a Principal. Permissions boundary or S C P (service control policy). Maximums that grant nothing on their own.

1.title: Policy structure
1.text: Policy structure. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Policy structure, continued
1.text: Policy structure, continued. Effect (Allow or Deny), Action (A P I calls), Resource (A R N s), Condition (optional rules), Principal (only in resource-based policies). Evaluation: everything is denied by default; an explicit Deny always wins; otherwise an Allow is needed (and S C P s and boundaries must also allow).

1.title: Building least privilege
1.text: Building least privilege. Start from nothing, add the specific actions and resources the job needs (name the bucket and prefix, not ); avoid "Action": "" and "Resource": "". Use conditions: source V P C (Virtual Private Cloud) endpoint, M F A (multi-factor authentication) present, secure transport only, tags, organization I D, time. Find what is really used: I A M Access Analyzer can generate a policy from CloudTrail activity, validate policies (warnings, errors) and report unused access; last accessed information shows unused permissions to remove. Test with the I A M policy simulator; review regularly; split broad roles by job (one role per pipeline). Use guardrails: S C P s and permissions boundaries cap what administrators can grant. Exam tip: "A managed policy gives too much access" to write a customer managed policy with only the needed actions on specific resources, and use Access Analyzer to generate it from activity.

1.title: Storing Application and Database Credentials
1.text: Storing Application and Database Credentials. Purpose. A W S Secrets Manager: Secrets (database credentials, A P I keys). A W S Systems Manager Parameter Store: Configuration values and secrets. Rotation. A W S Secrets Manager: Built-in automatic rotation (managed for R D S (Relational Database Service), Aurora, Redshift; Lambda for others). A W S Systems Manager Parameter Store: None built in. Encryption. A W S Secrets Manager: K M S (Key Management Service), always. A W S Systems Manager Parameter Store: SecureString uses K M S; plain String is not encrypted. Structure. A W S Secrets Manager: Secrets with versions and staging labels. A W S Systems Manager Parameter Store: Hierarchies ( or kestrel or prod or db or host), tiers (standard and advanced). Cost. A W S Secrets Manager: Charged per secret and A P I call. A W S Systems Manager Parameter Store: Standard parameters are free; advanced tier has a charge. Cross-account. A W S Secrets Manager: Resource policy. A W S Systems Manager Parameter Store: Limited (advanced tier sharing).

1.title: Storing Application and Database Credentials, continued
1.text: Storing Application and Database Credentials, continued. Pick it when. A W S Secrets Manager: Credentials must rotate. A W S Systems Manager Parameter Store: Plain configuration or secrets that do not need rotation at low cost. Access with I A M: the job's role gets secretsmanager:GetSecretValue (and K M S decrypt on the key) for that one secret; never put credentials in code, environment variables in clear text, job parameters or logs. Glue connections, Lambda, E C S (Elastic Container Service), E M R and Redshift can reference a secret. Exam tip: "Store database credentials that rotate automatically" to Secrets Manager. "Store non-secret configuration cheaply" to Parameter Store.

1.title: Database Authorization in Amazon Redshift
1.text: Database Authorization in Amazon Redshift. Authentication can be database users and passwords, I A M (temporary credentials), or federated identities (I A M Identity Center and identity providers). Authorization inside the database uses users, groups and roles:; Users and groups collect permissions; roles (role-based access control) are named sets of permissions that can be granted to users and other roles; superuser bypasses checks (avoid); grant and revoke on schemas, tables, views, functions and procedures, down to columns; default privileges apply to future objects.

1.title: Database Authorization in Amazon Redshift, continued
1.text: Database Authorization in Amazon Redshift, continued. Finer controls:; Column-level grants for sensitive columns; Row-level security (R L S) policies filter rows by user or role (for example a region); Dynamic data masking (D D M) hides or partly shows values (for example last four digits) by role without changing the data. Lake and external data: Redshift Spectrum and data sharing also use Lake Formation or I A M (below).

1.title: Database Authorization in Amazon Redshift, continued
1.text: Database Authorization in Amazon Redshift, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: "Analysts must see only some columns of a Redshift table" to column-level grant (or a view, or dynamic data masking). "Show only their region's rows" to row-level security.

1.title: Permissions through AWS Lake Formation
1.text: Permissions through A W S Lake Formation. The figure shows this: Lake Formation permissions: engines such as Athena, Redshift, E M R and Glue ask Lake Formation, which checks grants on databases, tables, columns and rows and vends temporary access to the S three data. A W S Lake Formation is a central place to grant and revoke access to data lake data in S three and tables in the Glue Data Catalog, instead of managing S three bucket policies and I A M per user.

2.title: Permissions through AWS Lake Formation, continued
2.text: Permissions through A W S Lake Formation, continued. What you can grant: database, table, column permissions (select, insert, describe, alter, drop), data location permissions (where new tables may point), and grant option. Fine-grained controls:; Column-level security: include or exclude columns; Row-level and cell-level security: data filters with a row filter expression and column list; L F (Lake Formation)-tags (tag-based access control): tag databases, tables and columns (sensitivity equals pii, domain equals finance) and grant by tag; scales to thousands of tables. Principals: I A M users and roles, I A M Identity Center and S A M L (Security Assertion Markup Language) identities, other accounts.

2.title: Permissions through AWS Lake Formation, continued
2.text: Permissions through A W S Lake Formation, continued. Works with: Amazon Athena, Redshift Spectrum, Amazon E M R, A W S Glue, Amazon QuickSight and others: the engine asks Lake Formation, which vends temporary credentials for only the allowed data. Cross-account sharing: grant to another account (using A W S R A M underneath); the recipient creates resource links in its own catalog. Turn it on: by default, catalog resources may be open to I A M (the IAMAllowedPrincipals group); to enforce Lake Formation permissions, revoke that default and register the S three location with Lake Formation. Both layers must allow: I A M must permit the call, Lake Formation must permit the data.

2.title: Permissions through AWS Lake Formation, continued
2.text: Permissions through A W S Lake Formation, continued. Auditing: CloudTrail logs Lake Formation grants and data access. Exam tip: "Different teams must see different columns and rows of the same lake tables, managed centrally" to A W S Lake Formation (data filters and L F-tags), not per-bucket policies.

2.title: Role-Based, Tag-Based and Attribute-Based Authorization
2.text: Role-Based, Tag-Based and Attribute-Based Authorization. The figure shows this: Authorization models: role-based (by job function), tag-based (by resource tags), and attribute-based (compare principal and resource attributes with one flexible policy).

2.title: Role-Based, Tag-Based and Attribute-Based Authorization, continued
2.text: Role-Based, Tag-Based and Attribute-Based Authorization, continued. Role-based (R B A C). How it decides: Job function to role or group with a fixed permission set. Example: FinanceAnalyst role may read invoices. Strength: Simple, easy to audit. Watch for: Role explosion as teams grow. Tag-based (T B A C). How it decides: Resource tags drive access (L F-tags, resource tags in policies). Example: Anyone with domain equals finance permission can read tables tagged domain equals finance. Strength: Scales with data; new tagged tables inherit access. Watch for: Tag governance: who may tag?

2.title: Role-Based, Tag-Based and Attribute-Based Authorization, continued
2.text: Role-Based, Tag-Based and Attribute-Based Authorization, continued. Attribute-based (A B A C). How it decides: Compare attributes of the principal and the resource and context. Example: Allow if the principal tag for team equals the resource tag for team. Strength: One policy for many teams; fewer policies. Watch for: Consistent tags are essential. Policy-based is the general idea: permissions come from policies attached to identities or resources. Combine them: roles for broad job functions, tags and attributes for fine, scalable control. Protect the tags: restrict who may create or change the tags that drive access. Exam tip: "Avoid creating a new policy for every team" to A B A C (attribute-based access control) with matching principal and resource tags. "Grant by data domain or sensitivity across the lake" to Lake Formation L F-tags.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Policy types: A W S managed (broad), customer managed (own, versioned, reusable), inline, resource-based, boundaries or S C P s (maximums). Evaluation: Default deny, explicit deny wins, otherwise an allow is required (and S C P or boundary must allow). Least privilege: Specific actions and A R N s (Amazon Resource Name), conditions, Access Analyzer (generate from CloudTrail, validate, unused access), last accessed, policy simulator. Credentials: Secrets Manager (rotation, per-secret charge) versus Parameter Store (config, free standard tier, SecureString, no rotation). Redshift: Users, groups, roles (R B A C), grant or revoke to column level, row-level security, dynamic data masking, avoid superuser. Lake Formation: Central grants on databases, tables, columns, rows (data filters), L F-tags, S three data locations. R B A C (role-based access control) or T B A C (tag-based access control) or A B A C: Roles by job; resource tags; compare principal and resource attributes (one policy, many teams).

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Finance analysts must query a Redshift table but must not see the card number column. What is the simplest approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Redshift supports column-level grant and dynamic data masking to hide sensitive columns by role.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Several teams query the same S three data lake tables with Athena and Redshift Spectrum. Each team may see only certain columns and rows, and the company wants central management. Which service should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Lake Formation centralizes permissions on catalog tables, columns and rows for engines such as Athena and Redshift Spectrum.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. An organization has dozens of teams and wants one I A M policy that lets each team access only resources tagged with its own team name. Which approach fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A B A C compares attributes of the principal and the resource, so one policy covers many teams.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Select two. Which two actions help create least-privilege policies? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Access Analyzer can build policies from actual usage, and last accessed information shows permissions that can be removed. Wildcard and shared admin permissions break least privilege.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all four answers. Question one: B. Question two: D. Question three: A. Question four: A and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
